how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Linux-based iptables or nftables firewall, list all ACCEPT rules on the INPUT chain and cross-reference against any associated application-layer inspection (e.g., conntrack helpers or nDPI). Ports with only ACCEPT and no helper constitute the list.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers -v | grep ACCEPT ; nft list ruleset | grep 'tcp dport\|udp dport' | grep -v 'ct state'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each ACCEPT rule showing a destination port without a corresponding conntrack helper or DPI module reference should have its port number added to this list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Cisco ASA or FTD access-list configuration file for permit entries that specify only port numbers without an associated inspection class-map or Snort rule binding.
how_to_obtain.command: show access-list | include permit.*eq ; show service-policy | include inspect
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL entries with 'permit tcp any any eq 443' or 'permit udp any any eq 53' that do not appear in an 'inspect' policy-map class should be listed as ports lacking protocol enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Fortinet FortiGate API to enumerate firewall policies, extract those with explicit service port objects and application set to 'none', and collect the port numbers.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://<fgt-ip>/api/v2/cmdb/firewall/policy?format=name|service|application|action' | python3 -c "import sys,json; [print(p['name'], p.get('service',''), p.get('application','')) for p in json.load(sys.stdin)['results'] if p.get('action')=='accept' and p.get('application')==[]]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies returned with empty application arrays but explicit service ports indicate those ports are enforced by port-matching only; collect those port numbers into this array.

option_description: Controls whether the load balancer or multi-homed firewall configuration guarantees that both the request and response packets for any given TCP/UDP connection always traverse the same stateful firewall instance. This is enforced through mechanisms such as source IP affinity (sticky sessions), ECMP with consistent flow hashing (5-tuple), or active/standby HA with no ECMP.
security_impact: The Rego rule `asymmetric_routing_breaking_stateful_inspection` fires when `asymmetric_routing_paths_present` is true AND neither `stateful_inspection_symmetry_enforced` nor `firewall_state_synchronization_enabled` is true. Without symmetry enforcement, return traffic may reach a firewall instance that has no record of the original connection, causing it to drop or—in permissive configurations—pass uninspected traffic, effectively bypassing stateful policy. This enables T1599 (Network Boundary Bridging) and T1090.003 (Multi-hop Proxy) attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On an F5 BIG-IP load balancer, inspect the virtual server and pool configuration for persistence profiles to confirm source-address or cookie persistence is applied, ensuring symmetric return paths.
how_to_obtain.command: tmsh list ltm virtual <vs-name> persist ; tmsh list ltm persistence source-addr
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The virtual server should reference a persistence profile (e.g., 'source_addr' with timeout > 0). Absence of any persistence profile indicates symmetry is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Cisco ASA in multi-context or active/active HA mode, verify that connection replication and traffic redirection ensure symmetric flows; check ECMP configuration on the upstream router.
how_to_obtain.command: show failover ; show route | include ECMP\|equal-cost ; show conn count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: In active/standby mode, failover should show 'Active' on one unit only. Presence of multiple equal-cost routes to the same destination without session affinity on the upstream router indicates symmetry is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console for an Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer, review Target Group stickiness settings and check routing algorithm.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Load Balancers > Select ALB/NLB > Listeners > View/Edit Rules > Target Group > Attributes > Stickiness: Enabled (LB-generated cookie or application-based)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Stickiness enabled with a duration aligned to session timeout ensures the same target (and thus same firewall path) handles the full flow. 'Flow hash' algorithm on NLB also qualifies.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the AWS CLI to describe load balancer target group attributes and confirm stickiness or flow-hash routing is configured.
how_to_obtain.command: aws elbv2 describe-target-group-attributes --target-group-arn <arn> | jq '.Attributes[] | select(.Key | contains("stickiness"))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show 'stickiness.enabled' = 'true' and a non-zero 'stickiness.lb_cookie.duration_seconds' or 'stickiness.app_cookie.duration_seconds' value.

option_description: Controls whether connection state tables are actively synchronized across all firewall instances in a cluster or multi-homed HA deployment. When enabled, any firewall node can inspect return traffic for connections initiated through a peer node, compensating for asymmetric routing without requiring strict traffic path symmetry.
security_impact: The Rego rule `asymmetric_routing_breaking_stateful_inspection` requires that at least one of `stateful_inspection_symmetry_enforced` or `firewall_state_synchronization_enabled` be true to avoid triggering when `asymmetric_routing_paths_present` is true. Without state synchronization and without symmetry enforcement, a firewall node receiving return traffic it did not process for the initial SYN will have no connection table entry, potentially dropping legitimate traffic or—if configured to fail-open—passing it without inspection. This creates an uninspected channel exploitable via T1599 and T1020.001 (Traffic Duplication).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Palo Alto NGFW HA pair, verify that HA configuration includes state synchronization (session sync) and confirm the sync status.
how_to_obtain.command: show high-availability state ; show high-availability transitions ; debug ha dump-peer-state
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'State synchronization: enabled' should appear in the HA state output. Session sync state should show 'synchronized' and not 'disabled' or 'out-of-sync'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Fortinet FortiGate HA cluster, display the HA configuration and session synchronization status.
how_to_obtain.command: get system ha ; diagnose sys ha dump-by vcluster ; diagnose sys session stat | grep syn
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'session-sync-dev' should reference a sync interface, and 'override' or 'session-pickup' should be 'enable'. The diagnose output should show active session replication counts greater than zero.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the firewall HA configuration file for session synchronization directives, particularly for Check Point ClusterXL or VRRP-based HA deployments.
how_to_obtain.command: cphaconf show ; cphaprob state ; fw tab -t connections -s
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Check Point ClusterXL should show 'Cluster Mode: High Availability (Active Up)' or 'Load Sharing' with 'State Synchronization: On'. The connections table should show consistent counts across cluster members.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Palo Alto Panorama or device web UI, verify HA session synchronization settings under Device > High Availability.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Device > High Availability > General > Setup: HA Enabled=Yes; Election Settings: check 'Session Synchronization' checkbox is checked; State Synchronization: verify sync interface is defined and status shows 'synchronized'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The HA dashboard should display both peers as 'synchronized' with a non-zero session count under 'Synchronized Sessions'. Any 'out-of-sync' status requires investigation.

option_description: Indicates whether the network topology introduces routing conditions where response (return) traffic may exit through a different physical interface, logical path, or firewall instance than the path used for the original request. Common causes include ECMP routing without session affinity, multi-homed firewalls with equal-cost static routes, and policy-based routing overrides.
security_impact: This attribute is the primary trigger condition in the `asymmetric_routing_breaking_stateful_inspection` Rego rule. When set to true and neither compensating control (`stateful_inspection_symmetry_enforced` or `firewall_state_synchronization_enabled`) is active, the exposure fires. Asymmetric routing breaks connection tracking, allowing packets to traverse the perimeter without complete stateful inspection, which adversaries can exploit for boundary bridging (T1599) or to chain multi-hop proxies (T1090.003) through paths the firewall cannot correlate as part of established flows.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On each firewall or router at the perimeter, display the routing table and identify any equal-cost multipath routes to the same destination prefix. Multiple next-hops for the same destination indicate ECMP and potential asymmetry.
how_to_obtain.command: ip route show ; ip route show table all | grep -E 'nexthop|ecmp' ; netstat -rn
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of multiple 'via' entries for the same prefix (e.g., 'nexthop via 10.0.0.1 weight 1 nexthop via 10.0.0.2 weight 1') confirms ECMP and potential asymmetric routing paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use traceroute in both directions (forward and reverse) between a known external test host and an internal host to determine if the return path differs from the forward path.
how_to_obtain.command: traceroute -n <internal-host-ip> ; mtr --report --no-dns --report-cycles 10 <internal-host-ip>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If forward and reverse traceroutes show different intermediate hops or different firewall IP addresses, asymmetric routing is confirmed. Symmetric paths show identical or mirrored hop sequences.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Cisco router or multilayer switch at the perimeter, check for ECMP or unequal-cost load balancing configuration using CEF or EIGRP variance.
how_to_obtain.command: show ip cef exact-route <src-ip> <dst-ip> ; show ip route <destination> ; show ip protocols | include maximum-paths
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If 'maximum-paths' is greater than 1 and the routing table shows multiple paths for the same prefix with equal administrative distance, ECMP is active and asymmetric routing is possible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture packets simultaneously on all perimeter firewall interfaces using tcpdump or a network tap, then send a test connection from an external source and verify that SYN and SYN-ACK traverse the same interface.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i any -w /tmp/capture.pcap 'host <test-external-ip>' & sleep 30 ; kill %1 ; tcpdump -r /tmp/capture.pcap | grep -E 'SYN|SYN-ACK' | awk '{print $1, $3, $5}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If SYN packets appear on interface eth0 but SYN-ACK packets appear on eth1, asymmetric routing is confirmed and the attribute should be set to true.

option_description: Controls whether the credentials (user accounts, service accounts, API keys, SSH keys, and secrets) used to administer boundary devices (firewalls, VPN gateways, load balancers) are stored and managed in a completely separate credential store from those used for internal zone systems. No shared accounts, reused passwords, or derivable secrets should exist between the boundary and internal planes.
security_impact: The Rego rule `boundary_credential_reuse_across_zones` fires when `credential_scope_separation_enforced` is false, either alone or in combination with `not boundary_to_internal_mfa_required`. If boundary device administrators use the same Active Directory accounts, SSH key pairs, or API tokens as internal system administrators, a perimeter compromise immediately yields valid credentials for internal zone pivot without any additional exploitation step. This directly enables T1078 (Valid Accounts) and T1110.004 (Credential Stuffing) for lateral movement from the perimeter to the internal zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the local user database from perimeter devices and compare against internal LDAP/AD users. On Palo Alto NGFW, list local admin accounts and compare against internal directory accounts.
how_to_obtain.command: show admins all ; show user group-mapping statistics ; show user ip-user-mapping all
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Boundary device admin accounts should reference a dedicated administrative OU or LDAP group (e.g., 'CN=FW-Admins,OU=PerimeterMgmt') that has zero overlap with internal application or server admin groups.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the IAM/PAM team to confirm whether a separate credential vault (e.g., CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault) is used exclusively for boundary device secrets, with distinct safe/path configurations and no cross-access policies allowing internal zone accounts to access boundary secrets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The team should be able to demonstrate separate vault safes/mounts (e.g., 'perimeter-devices/' vs. 'internal-infra/') with distinct LDAP or OIDC group bindings and no shared policies granting access to both.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the PAM solution API (e.g., CyberArk REST API) to list accounts in the perimeter boundary safe and cross-reference against accounts in internal infrastructure safes.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: <cyberark-token>' 'https://<pvwa-host>/PasswordVault/api/Accounts?filter=safeName eq PerimeterDevices' | jq '[.value[].userName]' ; curl -sk -H 'Authorization: <cyberark-token>' 'https://<pvwa-host>/PasswordVault/api/Accounts?filter=safeName eq InternalInfra' | jq '[.value[].userName]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The two lists should have zero overlapping usernames. Any username appearing in both lists indicates credential scope separation is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review RADIUS or TACACS+ configuration on boundary devices to confirm they authenticate to a dedicated AAA server or group policy that is not shared with internal device AAA policies.
how_to_obtain.command: show running-config | include aaa\|tacacs\|radius ; show tacacs
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The TACACS+ or RADIUS server group referenced by boundary devices should use a distinct server IP or a distinct group/realm from that used by internal network devices and servers.

option_description: Indicates whether a cross-referencing audit has confirmed that specific user accounts, service accounts, API keys, or SSH public keys concretely exist on both boundary devices and internal zone systems. Unlike scope separation enforcement (a policy control), this attribute reflects an empirical finding from evidence-based enumeration and comparison.
security_impact: The Rego rule `boundary_credential_reuse_across_zones` fires unconditionally when `shared_credential_identities_detected` is true, regardless of other controls. This is the most direct indicator of credential reuse risk. A confirmed shared identity means an attacker who extracts or bruteforces the credential from a boundary device (e.g., firewall management interface) can immediately authenticate to internal systems using the same identity token, enabling T1078 (Valid Accounts) lateral movement and T1589.001 (Credentials) reconnaissance exploitation without needing to perform additional credential theft steps internally.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract SSH authorized_keys from all boundary device admin accounts and compare their public key fingerprints against those in internal servers' authorized_keys files using a diff or intersection script.
how_to_obtain.command: for host in <fw1> <vpngw1> <lb1>; do ssh admin@$host 'cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /etc/ssh/authorized_keys.d/*' 2>/dev/null; done | sort -u > /tmp/boundary_keys.txt ; for host in <internal-host1> <internal-host2>; do ssh admin@$host 'cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys' 2>/dev/null; done | sort -u > /tmp/internal_keys.txt ; comm -12 /tmp/boundary_keys.txt /tmp/internal_keys.txt
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The comm -12 output should be empty. Any matching SSH public key fingerprints in both files confirm shared credential identities and this attribute should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate local user accounts on boundary devices and cross-reference against Active Directory or LDAP for accounts that also have internal system access rights.
how_to_obtain.command: ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<dc-ip> -D 'cn=auditor,dc=corp,dc=com' -W -b 'dc=corp,dc=com' '(memberOf=CN=FW-Admins,OU=PerimeterMgmt,DC=corp,DC=com)' sAMAccountName | grep sAMAccountName > /tmp/fw_users.txt ; ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<dc-ip> -D 'cn=auditor,dc=corp,dc=com' -W -b 'dc=corp,dc=com' '(memberOf=CN=Server-Admins,OU=Internal,DC=corp,DC=com)' sAMAccountName | grep sAMAccountName > /tmp/internal_users.txt ; comm -12 <(sort /tmp/fw_users.txt) <(sort /tmp/internal_users.txt)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No usernames should appear in both files. Any overlap means the same AD identity has both perimeter device and internal system membership, confirming shared credential identities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Compare API keys provisioned in the boundary device management APIs (e.g., Palo Alto API keys, F5 iControl tokens) against API keys stored in internal secrets managers or CI/CD systems.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk 'https://<fw-ip>/api/?type=keygen&user=<user>&password=<pass>' | grep key ; vault kv list secret/internal-api-keys | xargs -I{} vault kv get secret/internal-api-keys/{}
how_to_obtain.expected_output: API key values or associated metadata (e.g., labels, descriptions, owning service accounts) from boundary devices should have no matches in the internal secrets manager. Matching key values or service account names confirm shared identities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the operations team to identify any shared break-glass or emergency accounts that are provisioned on both boundary devices and internal management systems, including shared root or enable-mode passwords.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The team should confirm that break-glass accounts are unique per zone with distinct credentials, vaulted separately, and rotated independently. Any admission of shared emergency credentials confirms this attribute as true.

option_description: Controls whether an additional, distinct multi-factor authentication (MFA) challenge is required when a session that has already authenticated at the boundary layer (e.g., via VPN authentication or jump-host login) attempts to access or administer internal zone resources. This step-up authentication must be a separate MFA event, not simply inheriting the boundary authentication token.
security_impact: The Rego rule `boundary_credential_reuse_across_zones` fires when `credential_scope_separation_enforced` is false AND `boundary_to_internal_mfa_required` is false. Even if some credential reuse exists, a mandatory step-up MFA at the internal zone boundary forces an adversary who has compromised a boundary device credential to also compromise a second factor before reaching internal systems. Without this control, VPN authentication alone becomes sufficient to access internal management planes, enabling T1133 (External Remote Services) abuse and making T1078 (Valid Accounts) exploitation trivially scalable from the perimeter.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review VPN gateway policy assignments to confirm that post-VPN-authentication access to internal management networks (e.g., SSH to servers, RDP to workstations, access to management VLANs) requires an additional MFA step through a PAM gateway or step-up RADIUS challenge.
how_to_obtain.command: show vpn-sessiondb detail anyconnect | grep -E 'Auth-Method|Group-Policy|VLAN|MFA' ; show run group-policy <internal-access-policy> | include authentication
how_to_obtain.expected_output: VPN sessions destined for internal management subnets should route through a jump-host or PAM gateway that enforces a second authentication. Group policy should not grant direct management VLAN access post-single-factor VPN authentication.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the jump-host or bastion server PAM configuration (e.g., /etc/pam.d/sshd) to confirm an MFA module (e.g., pam_duo, pam_google_authenticator, pam_radius) is invoked for all internal-bound sessions.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/pam.d/sshd ; grep -r 'pam_duo\|pam_google_authenticator\|pam_radius' /etc/pam.d/ ; sshd -T | grep -E 'ChallengeResponseAuthentication|AuthenticationMethods'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The sshd PAM stack should include a 'required' or 'sufficient' line referencing an MFA module (e.g., 'auth required pam_duo.so'). The sshd_config AuthenticationMethods directive should require 'publickey,keyboard-interactive' or 'keyboard-interactive' to force MFA challenge even after key-based boundary authentication.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the Duo Security, Okta, or Azure AD Conditional Access admin console, verify that a policy enforcing MFA is applied specifically to applications or network locations representing internal management access, triggered even for already-authenticated VPN sessions.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Duo Admin > Policies > Create/Edit Policy: Applications = [SSH Gateway, Internal RDP Proxy] > 'Require Enrollment' and 'Require MFA' = Always; OR Azure AD > Security > Conditional Access > Policies: Conditions = Network Location (Internal Mgmt Subnet), Grant = Require MFA
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A conditional access or authentication policy should exist that explicitly covers internal management applications or network zones and mandates MFA regardless of the user's current VPN session state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Conduct a walkthrough with the operations or security team to trace the actual authentication flow from VPN login to internal server SSH or RDP access. Verify whether the team can reach internal management systems with only VPN credentials and no additional MFA prompt.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The walkthrough should demonstrate that after VPN authentication, reaching an internal server (e.g., via SSH to a production host or RDP to a domain controller) triggers a distinct MFA challenge (TOTP, push notification, hardware token). If internal access is reachable without any additional prompt, the attribute should be set to false.

option_description: Tracks the number of firewall rules that are completely unreachable because an earlier, broader rule in the ordered policy will always match first. These shadowed rules never execute, meaning their intended allow or deny behavior is silently bypassed, creating a gap between documented policy intent and enforced behavior.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the firewall_rule_shadowing_and_stale_policy exposure whenever shadowed_rule_count > 0. Shadowed deny rules are particularly dangerous because they create the illusion of a control that never fires, enabling attackers to exploit traffic paths the administrator believed were blocked. This maps to MITRE T1562.004 (Disable or Modify System Firewall) and T1562.007, where the effective policy diverges from the stated configuration without any explicit modification by an adversary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Tufin SecureTrack, AlgoSec FireFlow, or the open-source Firemon CLI to perform automated shadowing analysis against the exported ruleset. For iptables-based firewalls, pipe the ruleset through a shadow-detection script.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables-save | python3 /opt/tools/iptables_shadow_check.py --output-shadowed-count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer output such as 'Shadowed rules detected: 4' or a JSON object with a shadowed_count field.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Palo Alto Networks firewalls, export the security policy and run the policy optimizer via the CLI to identify rules with zero hit counts that are preceded by broader matching rules.
how_to_obtain.command: show security policy-optimizer rule-usage | match 'shadowed\|hit-count 0'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of rule names marked as shadowed or with 0 hits beneath a broader rule, enabling a count of affected entries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Cisco Firepower Management Center (FMC), navigate to Policies > Access Control, select the policy, then use the Analysis > Policy Analysis tab to review the Rule Conflict report, which explicitly flags shadowed rules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: FMC UI > Policies > Access Control > [Policy Name] > Analysis > Rule Conflict Report
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A table listing rules identified as shadowed, with the earlier conflicting rule cited, from which a count can be derived.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Palo Alto Panorama or firewall REST API to retrieve all security rules, then apply pairwise superset analysis programmatically to count shadowed entries.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'X-PAN-KEY: $API_KEY' 'https://<firewall>/restapi/v10.1/Policies/SecurityRules?location=vsys&vsys=vsys1' | jq '[.result.entry[] | select(."@shadowed" == "yes")] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing the count of rules the API or post-processing identifies as shadowed.

typical_values: 1–5 (common in mid-sized environments with moderate policy churn)
10–50 (typical in enterprises with unmanaged rule accumulation over years)
100+ (legacy environments with no formal policy lifecycle)

option_description: Counts the number of active firewall rules whose destination IP addresses, CIDR ranges, hostnames, or service ports no longer correspond to any active service or host according to the current IPAM or CMDB inventory. These rules persist after service decommission, potentially permitting traffic to IP ranges that have been reassigned to different, unrelated services in a different trust context.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the firewall_rule_shadowing_and_stale_policy exposure when stale_rule_count > 0, and also feeds the ingress_acl_misconfiguration exposure via stale_rules_present == true. A stale allow rule to a decommissioned server's former IP may now inadvertently permit access to a newly provisioned host at the same address in a different trust zone. This silently erodes zone separation and is directly exploitable under MITRE T1562.004 and T1070.007, where configuration drift obscures the true security posture.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Export the full firewall ruleset as a CSV or XML file and cross-reference each destination IP and port against the authoritative IPAM system (e.g., Infoblox, phpIPAM) and CMDB (e.g., ServiceNow). Flag rules with no matching active CI record.
how_to_obtain.command: python3 /opt/tools/stale_rule_checker.py --ruleset firewall_export.xml --ipam-api https://ipam.internal/api --cmdb-api https://cmdb.internal/api --output stale_rules.csv
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A CSV listing rule IDs, destination IPs, and whether each IP matches an active CMDB record; stale count is the number of unmatched rows.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On FortiGate firewalls, use the CLI to list all policy rules with zero hit counts, which are strong candidates for staleness. Combine with IPAM cross-reference to confirm decommission status.
how_to_obtain.command: diagnose firewall iprope show 00100004 | grep -E 'pkts=0|bytes=0' | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count of zero-hit rules. Each should then be validated against IPAM to confirm the destination is decommissioned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AlgoSec FireFlow or Tufin SecureTrack, navigate to the Rule Usage report and filter for rules with no traffic in the past 90 days. Cross-reference flagged rules against the CMDB to determine which reference decommissioned services.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AlgoSec AFA > Reports > Rule Usage > Filter: Last Used > 90 days ago
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of unused rules with last-hit timestamps, from which stale rules referencing decommissioned services can be counted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Infoblox IPAM API to retrieve all active host records, then compare against firewall rule destinations extracted via the firewall vendor API to identify rules with no matching active host.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$PASS 'https://infoblox.internal/wapi/v2.11/ipv4address?_return_fields=ip_address,status&status=USED' | jq '[.[].ip_address]' > active_ips.json && python3 compare_rules_to_ipam.py --rules fw_rules.json --active-ips active_ips.json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of firewall rules whose destination IPs do not appear in the active IPAM host list.

typical_values: 20–100 (typical in organizations lacking formal firewall lifecycle management)
200+ (large legacy environments where service decommissions are not tracked to firewall cleanup)

option_description: Measures the number of calendar days elapsed since the firewall ruleset or ACL was last formally reviewed, certified, and documented by an authorized reviewer. This value reflects policy review staleness independent of individual rule changes, capturing whether the overall policy has been holistically audited against current business and network requirements.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the firewall_rule_shadowing_and_stale_policy exposure when rule_review_age_days > 180 AND automated_shadow_detection_enabled is false. Without periodic formal review, shadowed and stale rules accumulate silently, and the policy drifts from business intent. Extended review gaps allow conditions supporting MITRE T1562.004 and T1070.007 to persist undetected, where effective policy modification or configuration obscurity undermines boundary enforcement over time.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the organization's change management ticketing system (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira) for the most recent closed ticket categorized as a firewall policy recertification or annual review. Calculate the difference between today's date and the ticket close date.
how_to_obtain.command: date -d $(curl -sk -u admin:$TOKEN 'https://servicenow.internal/api/now/table/change_request?sysparm_query=category%3Dfirewall_review%5Estate%3Dclosed&sysparm_limit=1&sysparm_fields=closed_at&sysparm_orderby=closed_at%3ADESC' | jq -r '.result[0].closed_at[:10]') '+%s' | xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo $(( ($(date +%s) - {}) / 86400 ))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing the number of days since the last review ticket was closed. A value over 180 is a policy trigger condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall policy documentation or metadata file maintained by the network security team. Many organizations embed a review date field in the policy export header or a companion governance document.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'last.?reviewed|certified.?date|review.?date' /etc/firewall/policy_metadata.txt
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A date string such as 'Last Reviewed: 2023-06-15' from which days elapsed can be calculated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Tufin SecureTrack, navigate to the Policy Compliance module and view the Recertification Campaign history to find the most recently completed campaign and its completion date.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Tufin SecureTrack > Policy > Compliance > Recertification Campaigns > Completed
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of completed recertification campaigns with end dates; the most recent end date determines rule_review_age_days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Check Point firewalls, query the SmartConsole database for the last policy install timestamp as a proxy for the last review if no formal recertification record exists, then calculate elapsed days.
how_to_obtain.command: cpstat mg -f policy | grep 'Policy install time' | awk '{print $NF}' | xargs -I{} bash -c 'echo $(( ($(date +%s) - $(date -d "{}" +%s)) / 86400 )) days'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer number of days since the last policy install, usable as a lower-bound estimate of review age if no formal record exists.

typical_values: 0–90 (mature security programs with quarterly review cycles)
181–365 (common in organizations without formal recertification programs; triggers policy finding)
365+ (high-risk state seen in legacy environments; indicates no structured review process)

option_description: Indicates whether an automated policy analysis tool or CI/CD-integrated process is actively and continuously or periodically scanning the firewall ruleset to detect shadowed, redundant, or stale rules and generating alerts or reports on findings. When enabled, this control compensates for human review gaps by ensuring rule quality issues surface without waiting for a manual audit cycle.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates automated_shadow_detection_enabled as a compensating control: when it is false and rule_review_age_days > 180, the firewall_rule_shadowing_and_stale_policy exposure is triggered even in the absence of confirmed shadowed or stale rules. This reflects that without automation, the organization has no continuous assurance that the policy is clean between manual reviews. Absence of this control sustains blind spots exploitable via MITRE T1562.004 and T1562.007, where policy drift goes undetected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network security or firewall administration team to determine whether a tool such as AlgoSec, Tufin, Firemon, or a custom script is integrated into the change management pipeline and actively running scheduled rule analysis jobs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation of a named tool, its scan frequency (e.g., daily, on every rule change), and evidence that alerts are routed to an active queue or SIEM.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AlgoSec AFA, navigate to Administration > Scheduled Tasks and verify that a rule analysis job is configured, enabled, and has a recent last-run timestamp confirming it is actively executing.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AlgoSec AFA > Administration > Scheduled Tasks > Rule Analysis Jobs
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one active scheduled analysis job with a last-run time within the expected scan interval (e.g., within the last 24 hours for daily jobs).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the CI/CD pipeline (e.g., Jenkins, GitLab CI) for a pipeline definition that includes a firewall policy linting or shadow detection stage, confirming it runs on every policy change commit.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GITLAB_TOKEN' 'https://gitlab.internal/api/v4/projects/<id>/pipelines?status=success&ref=main' | jq '[.[].id] | length' && curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GITLAB_TOKEN' 'https://gitlab.internal/api/v4/projects/<id>/repository/files/.gitlab-ci.yml/raw?ref=main' | grep -i 'shadow\|firewall-lint\|tufin\|algosec'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A CI/CD pipeline YAML file containing a stage referencing a shadow detection tool, confirming automated integration. Zero matches indicates the control is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for a cron job or scheduled task definition on the firewall management server that invokes a rule analysis script or API call to a policy management platform.
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l -u fwadmin | grep -iE 'shadow|stale|policy.?analysis|algosec|tufin|firemon' && ls -la /etc/cron.d/ | grep -iE 'firewall|policy'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A cron entry invoking a rule analysis command or script, with a schedule indicating regular execution. No output confirms the absence of automated detection.

typical_values: false (common default; organizations relying solely on manual periodic review)
true (mature security programs with policy management platforms integrated into change workflows)
